text: Redis AOF has three fsync policies: always (very slow, safest), everysec (the default; 'you may lose 1 second of data'), and no (the OS flushes, typically every 30 s on Linux). Redis recommends combining AOF with periodic RDB snapshots for backups and faster restarts.
why: Turns 'configure AOF' into the concrete durability knob a learner must set.

text: Redis replication is asynchronous by default; even WAIT 'does not turn a set of Redis instances into a CP system': acknowledged writes can still be lost during a failover.
why: Using Redis as a primary DB needs this caveat about failover data loss.

text: Redis 'expired' events are generated when Redis actually deletes the key, either on access or by an incremental background sweep, so there can be a significant delay after the TTL reaches zero. Keyspace notifications are disabled by default (notify-keyspace-events) and are fire-and-forget Pub/Sub.
why: The online/offline design relies on expiry hooks; learners must know they are late and lossy.

text: DynamoDB TTL deletes expired items 'typically within a few days' without consuming write capacity, and expired-but-not-yet-deleted items still show up in reads unless filtered out. Deletions appear in DynamoDB Streams as service deletions.
why: Quantifies why DynamoDB TTL cannot drive a real-time offline signal.

text: AWS SDKs reuse TCP connections (HTTP keep-alive) by default; AWS notes that for short DynamoDB queries a new TCP connection can cost more than the query itself.
why: Corrects the idea that DynamoDB clients cannot hold persistent connections.

text: DynamoDB typically responds in single-digit milliseconds; DAX, an in-memory cache in front of it, cuts eventually consistent reads to microseconds.
why: Gives the actual latency numbers behind the Redis vs DynamoDB comparison.

text: Redis moved from BSD to source-available RSALv2/SSPLv1 in March 2024, and Redis 8 (May 2025) added the OSI-approved AGPLv3 as an option. AWS and Google meanwhile back Valkey, a BSD-licensed fork, which ElastiCache now offers alongside Redis OSS.
why: The 'Redis is open source' argument for avoiding lock-in depends on this licensing history.

text: Since Redis 8, Redis Open Source includes probabilistic types (Bloom and Cuckoo filters, Count-min sketch, Top-K, t-digest), JSON, time series and vector sets, alongside HyperLogLog and geospatial indexes.
why: Clarifies which 'advanced data structures' are built in today.

text: In InnoDB a DELETE does not physically remove the row immediately: the row and its index records are removed later by purge, once no transaction needs them for MVCC or rollback. In PostgreSQL, likewise, 'an UPDATE or DELETE of a row does not immediately remove the old version'; VACUUM reclaims it.
why: Corrects the mental model that each hard delete immediately restructures the tree.

text: InnoDB tries to merge an index page with a neighbour only when the page's fill falls below MERGE_THRESHOLD (default 50%), after a delete or a row-shortening UPDATE. The threshold is configurable per table or per index.
why: This is the actual 'rebalancing' trigger in the most common B+ tree engine.

text: MySQL suggests DELETE ... LIMIT row_count, repeated until fewer rows are affected, so no single DELETE runs too long. For very large purges it also suggests copying the rows to keep into a new table and swapping it in with RENAME TABLE.
why: Gives the concrete SQL pattern for staggered deletes.

text: PostgreSQL partial unique indexes enforce uniqueness only for rows matching a WHERE clause, e.g. CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON users(email) WHERE NOT is_deleted. Soft-deleted rows then no longer block re-registration with the same email.
why: Shows soft delete and uniqueness can coexist.

text: MongoDB TTL indexes are enforced by a background thread in mongod that runs every 60 seconds, so documents can outlive their expiry by a minute or more under load.
why: Concrete example of offloading the deletion job to the database.

text: In InnoDB's DYNAMIC row format (the default), long VARCHAR/TEXT/BLOB values move fully off-page behind a 20-byte pointer only when the row is too long for the page; TEXT/BLOB values of 40 bytes or less always stay inline.
why: Refines 'long text is always stored separately' with the actual rule.

text: PostgreSQL has no short/long text split: TOAST compresses or moves any wide value out of line once the row exceeds about 2 kB. Out-of-line values are fetched only if the query selects them.
why: The same idea in the other major open-source engine, with different mechanics.

text: InnoDB's maximum in-page row size is slightly under half a page (just under 8 KB with the default 16 KB pages), and MySQL caps any row at 65,535 bytes. TEXT/BLOB columns count only 9-12 bytes toward that limit because their contents are stored separately.
why: Gives the actual limits behind 'row length has to be limited'.

text: In MySQL, utf8mb4 characters can need up to 4 bytes, so a VARCHAR/TEXT length in characters can be up to 4x as many bytes.
why: Corrects the characters = bytes assumption used in the sizing example.

text: MySQL storage sizes (5.6.4+): DATE 3 bytes, DATETIME 5 bytes, TIMESTAMP 4 bytes, plus 0-3 bytes for fractional seconds. DATETIME covers 1000-01-01 to 9999-12-31.
why: Replaces the hedged '6 bytes' and range recollection with the documented figures.

text: PostgreSQL timestamp and timestamptz take 8 bytes and span 4713 BC to 294276 AD at 1-microsecond resolution; date takes 4 bytes.
why: This is the 'huge range in few bytes' example the teacher was reaching for.

text: MySQL TIMESTAMP, a 4-byte epoch-based type, ends at '2038-01-19 03:14:07' UTC, the same Year-2038 limit that hits any signed 32-bit epoch-seconds column.
why: Gives the exact overflow date with a real-world type that has it.

text: MySQL converts TIMESTAMP values to UTC for storage and back to the session time zone on retrieval, while DATETIME stores no zone at all. PostgreSQL timestamptz stores UTC and does not keep the original zone.
why: Native types usually do not preserve the user's time zone; store it separately if needed.

text: SQLite has no date/time storage class: dates are stored as ISO-8601 TEXT, REAL Julian day numbers or INTEGER Unix time, and the application chooses which.
why: A real database where 'dates as strings' is a common default.

text: India's IT Rules 2021 require intermediaries to retain removed information and user-registration records for 180 days for investigation purposes, and to provide information to authorised agencies within 72 hours of an order.
why: Gives the legal basis behind 'we have to provide this information' for Indian consumer platforms.

text: GDPR Art. 17 gives data subjects a right to erasure of their personal data. Art. 17(3) exempts processing needed for a legal obligation or for legal claims, which is why audit-retention is defensible but ML archival of deleted content needs its own legal basis.
why: Separates lawful audit retention from optional archival.

text: MongoDB supports multi-document ACID transactions on replica sets since 4.0 and on sharded clusters since 4.2. Its docs note that single-document operations are already atomic and that embedding often removes the need for transactions.
why: Pins versions to the 'MongoDB supports ACID' claim.
